job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jamal, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the IT help desk at a regional insurance company in Corvale. I studied information systems, and for my final project I built a small claims-tracking database for a charity. All day I reset passwords, fix laptops, and chase down why a claims screen froze. I share a flat with my friend Kofi, who's an apprentice plumber, and on Saturday mornings I coach an under-12 football team. I'd like to get into network or systems engineering one day, but the help desk is where the entry jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a handy tool and nothing more. At work I'd say the help desk will always need a person who can walk up to your desk and look at your screen. To the football parents I'd say not to worry, the kids will still need to learn to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd say good, but I'm not relaxed. My loan is big and my pay is low. If the insurer has a bad year, they'd trim contractors and juniors first, and I'm on a one-year graduate contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard, and ask my manager Teodora about a path from help desk to systems admin. I'd study for a networking certificate at night, which costs about 300. I'd also stay at my coaching job on Saturdays, because it keeps me sane and I'm good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little tight about the contract, but I'm used to making the best of what I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your graduate contract isn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my contract wasn't renewed, I'd look for work at the university or the hospital, which both have IT teams. Few openings, but they exist. I'd also ask my uncle Emeka, who runs a small shop, if I could do his computers for pocket money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell the kids you coach about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd tell the under-12s is that a job is something you earn by turning up and trying. I know it's a bit old-fashioned, but it's what I believe.

say: I'd say it's a **handy tool** and nothing more.
At work I'd say the help desk will always need a **person** who can look at your screen.
think: I'm not **relaxed**, because my loan is big and my pay is low.
The insurer would trim **juniors** first in a bad year, and I'm on a one-year contract.
do: Ask my manager **Teodora** about a path from help desk to systems admin.
Study for a **networking certificate** at night, costing about 300.
feel: I feel **fine**, mostly, a little tight about the contract.
S0.quote: A job is something you earn by turning up and trying. I know it's a bit old-fashioned, but it's what I believe.
fieldNote: Jamal frames work as a **moral matter**, earned by effort, which matches his traditional views.
His real risk is the one-year contract and the loan, not AI.
He has small, real fallback options through the university, hospital and his uncle's shop.

steps.text: Ask Teodora about a path from help desk to systems admin
Study for a 300-pound networking certificate at night
Keep coaching the under-12s every Saturday
Apply to the university and hospital IT teams if the contract ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that it's a big change and people should be given a fair chance to adapt. At work I'd tell Teodora that help desk tasks like password resets and ticket sorting are the first things the company will hand to software. I'd say that firms should train their own people rather than hire from outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is in the line of fire. A chatbot can answer half of what I answer, and the rest are things like swapping a dead laptop, which a person still does. If the insurer cuts the help desk from six people to three, I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the company's AI assistant straight away and learn how it works, because when they move to it I'll be the person who knows. I'd steer my work toward the hands-on side, like setting up laptops and network equipment. And I'd speed up the networking certificate, then apply for junior system admin roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pressed, but not panicked. Like a football match where the other side has scored first, but there's still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Gwen has been at the desk for 14 years and she hates the new tools. I worry for her more than me. She's the heart of the team, and the company might not see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help her by sitting beside her and walking through the AI assistant. I'd also tell Teodora that people like Gwen are worth keeping, because they know every person in the building.

say: I'd say people need a **fair chance** to adapt, and firms should train their own staff.
I'd say password resets and ticket sorting go to **software** first.
think: A chatbot can answer **half** of what I answer, and I'm the newest of six.
The hands-on parts, like swapping a dead laptop, **stay** with people.
do: Try the company's **AI assistant** straight away to learn it before others.
Move my work toward **hardware** and network equipment.
Speed up the networking **certificate** and apply for junior sysadmin roles.
feel: I feel **pressed**, not panicked, like a match where the other side scored first.
S1.quote: My colleague Gwen has been at the desk for 14 years and she hates the new tools.
fieldNote: Jamal is **practical and loyal**: learn the tool early, move to hardware, and look out for older colleagues.
He identifies the exposed tasks plainly and assigns himself the newest-in, first-out risk.
His football comparison shows his steady attitude under pressure.

steps.text: Learn the company's AI assistant before the rest of the desk
Take on laptop and network equipment setup work
Finish the networking certificate and apply for junior sysadmin jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is far too fast for ordinary families. I'd say that the government has to protect people while this happens, but I wouldn't want only handouts. I'd want paid training and jobs, and I'd tell the football parents to talk to their children about trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. My whole job is answering questions, which is exactly what AI does best. I have a loan, a small flat and no savings, so I'd need to find another way to earn within a year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything extra and put 70 percent of my pay in savings. I'd talk to Kofi about getting into a trade, like plumbing or electrical, since robots take three more years to do that well. I'd ask my uncle Emeka for any work in his shop. And I'd go to my church and ask what help is available, while expecting to give some back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a little ashamed, which I know is odd. I did what I was told, and I still feel it's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell my parents everything. They worked hard so I'd have an office job. I'd say I'm exploring a trade, which is true, but not that I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a trade appeal to you or does it feel like a defeat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a trade would be good for me. I like fixing things, and I've fixed half the laptops in my building. It's just that it would be a different life than the one I planned.

say: I'd say the government should **protect people**, but with paid training and jobs, not only handouts.
I'd tell football parents to talk to their children about **trades**.
think: My whole job is answering questions, which AI does **best**.
I have a loan, a small flat and **no savings**, so I'd need another income within a year.
do: Cut everything extra and save **70 percent** of my pay.
Talk to Kofi about a **trade**, like plumbing or electrical.
Ask my uncle **Emeka** for work in his shop.
feel: I feel **frightened** and a little ashamed, though I did what I was told.
S2.quote: I like fixing things, and I've fixed half the laptops in my building.
fieldNote: Jamal feels **shame** as well as fear, which links to his belief that people earn their place by work.
He moves toward trades without much resistance, since he already enjoys fixing things.
He plans to hide his fear from his parents and ask his church, uncle and flatmate for help.

steps.text: Save 70 percent of my pay each month
Ask Kofi how to apply for a plumbing or electrical apprenticeship
Ask my uncle Emeka for work in his shop
Cut every extra cost like takeaways and the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is something we can work with. I'd say we should use it to build apprenticeships and local jobs, and that families and churches should help neighbours. At work I'd say we should train staff for jobs the company will still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel reasonably okay, though I'd keep my eyes open. By 2031 I'd be 27, ideally with a systems qualification and a small stash. I'd probably have a wife and a child too, if things go well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my networking certificate and aim for a systems admin job within two years. I'd save 120 a month and put another 60 toward the loan. I'd also stay on the football coaching, because teaching young people is a skill I'd like to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, and a little proud. It's like being told you've got time to train for a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you doubt a government training scheme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd be unsure about is whether the training the government offers would be any good. I've seen schemes where you get a certificate and no job. I'd rather do an apprenticeship with a firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a pay cut to move into the systems team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could, I'd ask my current firm to take me on formally for the systems team. I'd do it for less money, as long as I'm learning.

say: I'd say five years is **workable**, and we should build apprenticeships and local jobs.
At work I'd suggest training staff for jobs the company will still **need**.
think: By 2031 I'd be 27, ideally with a **systems** qualification and a small stash.
I'd keep my **eyes open**, even if I'm reasonably okay.
do: Finish the networking certificate and aim for a **systems admin** job in two years.
Save **120** a month and put 60 toward the loan.
feel: I feel **hopeful** and a little proud, like having time to train for a race.
S3.quote: I've seen schemes where you get a certificate and no job. I'd rather do an apprenticeship with a firm.
fieldNote: Jamal wants **apprenticeships with firms**, not classroom schemes, in line with his traditional, work-first views.
He would trade pay for learning inside the systems team.
His mood stays anxious because the help desk is still the exposed rung.

steps.text: Finish the networking certificate and apply for systems admin jobs
Save 120 a month and put 60 toward the loan
Ask my firm to move me into the systems team, even at lower pay
Keep coaching the under-12s on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time. I'd say we should treat it as a chance to prepare properly, with apprenticeships, family support and local business. There's no need to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I'd be 32 and well into my career. I'd have a qualification, a stable job and probably a family. I'd keep up with the technology, but I'd wait until it's proven before I changed how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study for a systems qualification and work up to a systems engineer role. I'd marry, save for a deposit and buy a small house in Corvale, ideally near my parents. I'd also coach football until my own children are old enough to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I think. It's a bit like knowing the season's fixtures in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for over the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd keep an eye on is the cost of living. If the jobs exist but houses cost twice as much, we're no better off. I'd want the government to look at housing, not just jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also keep my savings simple, in a bank and not in anything risky. My dad always said that you don't gamble with what your family lives on.

say: I'd say ten years is a chance to prepare **properly**, with apprenticeships and local business.
I'd say there's no need to **panic**.
think: At 32 I'd be well into my career with a **qualification**, a stable job and probably a family.
I'd wait until new technology is **proven** before changing how I work.
do: Study for a **systems** qualification and work up to systems engineer.
Marry, save a **deposit** and buy a small house in Corvale.
Keep my savings **simple**, in a bank, not in anything risky.
feel: I feel **settled**, like knowing the season's fixtures in advance.
S4.quote: If the jobs exist but houses cost twice as much, we're no better off.
fieldNote: Jamal turns to **housing costs** as the real long-term worry, even in a decade of notice.
He wants to wait for technology to be proven, matching his steady adaptability.
Uneasy, not calm, because his debt and thin cushion stay for years.

steps.text: Study for a systems qualification and aim for systems engineer
Keep savings in a plain bank account for a house deposit
Marry and buy a small house near my parents
Back candidates who tackle housing costs at the next election

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My help desk job is the first to go, and I don't have the savings or the time to change. What would help is real apprenticeships with firms, a warning from the company and a government that backs work, not just support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd rather earn than receive. People my age want the chance to work and build something. If you give us that, we'll do the rest.

headlineQuote: I'd rather earn than receive. People my age want the chance to work and build something.
portrait: Jamal is a **help desk** analyst at a regional insurer on a one-year graduate contract, sharing a flat with a plumber apprentice.
He is **traditional**, values work, family and community, and coaches an under-12 football team on Saturdays.
He's **steady**: learns new tools once colleagues have, and prefers apprenticeships to classroom schemes.
Shame and fear rise at two years, when his **trade** option becomes serious.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his help desk job goes first and he has neither savings nor time.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** with firms, early warning from his company and a government that backs work.
